issues.legal_issue: A written notice given before a change in the governing rent-control framework can satisfy the notice requirement for a later fair-rent proceeding without a fresh notice.
material_facts: The tenant gave the landlord written notice before filing an initial fair-rent suit under the then-existing framework.
After the governing framework changed, the initial plaint was returned for want of jurisdiction and the tenant filed a fresh proceeding before the Rent Controller without giving another notice.
The courts below treated the earlier notice as proper, and the Supreme Court found no basis to hold it insufficient.
issues.conclusion: The earlier notice was sufficient; the governing provision did not require that notice be issued in a particular form or after the new framework came into force.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(2) of the United State of Gwalior, Indore and Malwa (Madhya Bharat) Accommodation Control Act, Samvat 2006 requires notice in writing but prescribes neither a particular form nor that notice be given after the Act came into force. The Court relied on the provision's text and cited no earlier cases on this point.

predicates.fair_rent_fixation_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding to have rent fixed for accommodation.
predicates.written_notice_given_before_first_filing: The party seeking rent fixation gave the other party written notice before filing the initial proceeding.
predicates.first_plaint_returned_after_governing_fr: The governing framework changed after the initial proceeding was filed, and the initial plaint was returned before a fresh proceeding was filed.

issues.definition: When a fair-rent proceeding follows a returned initial plaint and the party had already given written notice, that earlier notice satisfies the notice requirement even though it preceded the change in the governing framework.

issues.legal_issue: A fair-rent order fairly construed to operate prospectively does not preserve civil-court jurisdiction over rent fixation after jurisdiction has shifted to the Rent Controller.
material_facts: The initial fair-rent suit was filed before the governing framework changed.
After the change, the initial plaint was returned and a fresh fair-rent proceeding was filed before the Rent Controller.
The Rent Controller's order, fairly construed, operated prospectively rather than from the beginning of the lease.
The High Court considered the suit's relation to a pre-change period a reason the civil-court plaint should not have been returned.
issues.conclusion: The Rent Controller's order was prospective, and after the governing framework changed, jurisdiction over rent fixation lay with the Rent Controller rather than the civil court; the argument that the plaint should not have been returned had no substance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the Rent Controller's order as prospective and held that, after the Accommodation Control Act came into operation, jurisdiction over rent fixation was vested in the Rent Controller, not the civil court. No earlier cases were cited for this point.

predicates.fair_rent_fixation_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding to have rent fixed for accommodation.
predicates.governing_framework_changed_before_fresh: The governing framework for rent fixation changed before the fresh proceeding was filed.
predicates.rent_controller_order_construed_as_prosp: The rent-fixing order was fairly construed to operate prospectively rather than from the beginning of the tenancy.

issues.definition: If a rent-fixation proceeding is brought after the governing framework changes and the resulting order operates prospectively, jurisdiction over that post-change rent fixation belongs to the Rent Controller.
